common_name: John May's Special Society Garlic (Robust Large-Flowered Tulbaghia)

planting.note: Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun in spring; this larger-growing selection benefits from a sheltered site or container culture where winters run colder than zone 8.

directions: John May's Special is a robust selection of society garlic that outgrows the common form in nearly every dimension, producing thicker, wider gray-green leaves and noticeably larger, more crowded umbels of rosy-violet flowers held on taller stems. Because the extra size and vigor come at some cost to cold tolerance, treat it as reliably hardy only in zone 8 and warmer, and mulch heavily or grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover during hard freezes farther north. Plant divisions in average, well-drained soil in full sun and expect a fuller, showier flowering display through the warm months than the species typically offers on the same footprint. Established clumps benefit from division every few years both to control size and to renew vigorous bloom.

common_name: Purple Star Tulbaghia (Large-Flowered Hybrid Society Garlic)

planting.note: Plant divisions in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun in spring; give plants at the cooler edge of zone 8 a sheltered site or winter mulch, since this hybrid is less cold-tested than straight T. violacea.

directions: Purple Star is a hybrid tulbaghia selected for markedly larger flower umbels and a richer violet-purple color than typical Society Garlic, giving it a bolder presence in the border despite a similarly compact, grassy clump of gray-green leaves. It flowers over an extended season, often nearly continuously in mild coastal climates, and like its parents releases a mild onion-garlic scent when the foliage is bruised or cut. Grow it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where it tends to perform more reliably than in rich, wet ground. Because it is less cold-tested than straight T. violacea, gardeners at the cooler edge of zone 8 should give it a sheltered site or winter mulch.

planting.note: Plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil in full sun in spring; culture matches the species, and heavy mulch protects the clump through winter in zone 7-8 gardens.

directions: Alba is a white-flowered selection of society garlic, replacing the species' violet-pink umbels with clusters of clean white, star-shaped flowers held above the same narrow, gray-green, faintly garlic-scented foliage. The pale flowers read as a soft accent rather than a strong color statement, making Alba useful for moon gardens, white borders, and pairing with pastel-flowered companions where the usual magenta-violet society garlic would clash. Culture is identical to the species: plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and expect nearly nonstop bloom from late spring through fall in zone 9 gardens. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering strong.

common_name: Taney Longwood Water Canna (Coral-Orange True Aquatic Canna)

planting.note: Set divided rhizomes in heavy aquatic soil in a submerged basket at the pond margin once the water has warmed after last frost, keeping the crown covered by a few inches of water.

directions: Taney is one of a handful of true aquatic canna hybrids bred at Longwood Gardens to grow with their rhizomes permanently submerged rather than merely in moist soil, a trait that sets it apart from ordinary garden canna cultivars that rot under constant flooding. It carries coral-orange flowers over green foliage on a plant sized for the middle of a pond planting, more compact than the tallest Longwood water canna selections. Set divided rhizomes in heavy aquatic soil in a submerged planting basket at the pond margin once the water has warmed following the last frost, and keep the crown covered by a few inches of water through the growing season. Where winters bring hard freezes, lift and store the rhizome indoors like a standard garden canna.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: His Majesty Longwood Water Canna (Tall Deep Red True Aquatic Canna)

planting.note: Set divided rhizomes in fertile aquatic soil in a submerged basket at the back of a pond planting once the water has warmed after last frost.

directions: His Majesty is the tallest and most imposing of the Longwood Gardens aquatic canna hybrids, bearing large, deep red flowers well above the water line on a plant that dwarfs sibling selections such as Taney and Erebus. Like the other Longwood water cannas, its rhizome is bred to tolerate permanent submersion at the pond margin rather than the merely moist soil that ordinary garden canna requires. Plant divided rhizomes in fertile aquatic soil in a submerged basket in full sun after the water has warmed in spring, siting it toward the back of a pond planting where its height can be appreciated without shading smaller marginal plants. In climates with hard winter freezes, bring the rhizome indoors for winter storage as with any tender canna.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening
International Waterlily and Water Gardening Society

common_name: Journey's End Canna (Dark Bronze-Purple Foliage Orange-Red Flowered Canna)

planting.note: Plant divided rhizomes in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed; the darkest leaf color develops with maximum sun exposure.

directions: Journey's End pairs dark bronze-purple foliage with bright orange-red flowers, a high-contrast combination that makes the leaf color as much a feature of the planting as the bloom itself. The foliage holds its dark pigment best in full sun, fading toward green in shadier spots, so give it the sunniest position available for the strongest color contrast. Plant divided rhizomes in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil and feed regularly through the growing season, since heavily pigmented cultivars are typically vigorous feeders that respond well to fertility. In zone 7 and cooler areas of its range, mulch the rhizomes heavily for winter or lift and store them like dahlia tubers.

common_name: Pink Sunburst Canna (Cream-and-Pink Striped Variegated Foliage Canna)

planting.note: Plant divided rhizomes in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun once the soil has warmed; variegation is most vivid on new growth produced in strong sun.

directions: Pink Sunburst carries broad leaves striped in cream, green, and rose-pink, a softer and more pastel-toned variegation than the maroon-and-green striping of better-known cultivars such as Tropicanna, topped by clear pink flowers that echo the pink foliage stripe. The variegation is most vivid on new growth in full sun; some fading toward green can occur on older leaves or in shadier sites. Grow it in rich, evenly moist soil and divide congested clumps every few years, since crowding can reduce both flowering and the crispness of the leaf variegation. It performs best as a container or border accent where its striped foliage can be viewed up close.

common_name: Constitution Canna (Giant Dark Purple-Black Leaf Pink-Flowered Canna)

planting.note: Plant divided rhizomes in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun once the soil has warmed, and feed generously through summer to support its unusually large leaves.

directions: Constitution is grown chiefly for its exceptionally large, glossy, near-black-purple leaves, which reach a scale unusual even among big-leaved canna cultivars and give the plant a substantial, almost banana-like presence in the border. The clear pink flowers, produced above the foliage through the warm season, are almost secondary to the dramatic leaf color and size. Because the huge leaves demand steady moisture and fertility to avoid scorching or stunting, plant divided rhizomes in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun and feed generously through summer. Give it plenty of room, since a well-fed clump can rival small shrubs in bulk by late summer.
